parsed_answer.content:
The Generational Garbage Collection model is a cornerstone of JVM memory management, capitalizing on the weak generational hypothesis: the empirical observation that the vast majority of objects die shortly after creation. By partitioning the heap into distinct physical regions based on object age, the JVM optimizes collection cycles, drastically reducing pause times (stop-the-world events). The Young Generation is where all new object allocations occur. It is further subdivided into an Eden space and two Survivor spaces (Survivor 0 and Survivor 1, or S0 and S1). Because most objects are short-lived, garbage collection in the Young Generation (known as a Minor GC) is extremely frequent and efficient, sweeping away dead objects while copying surviving ones between the Survivor spaces.

Over time, objects that survive multiple Minor GC cycles are promoted to the Old Generation, also known as the Tenured Generation. The Old Gen houses long-lived objects, such as Spring beans, application caches, and singleton instances. Because objects here have already proven their longevity, they are expected to remain alive for a long time. Collections in this region (Major GC or Full GC) are significantly more expensive and time-consuming because the Old Gen occupies a much larger portion of the heap and requires complex compaction algorithms to prevent severe memory fragmentation.

rows: Initial allocation site for newly created Java objects
Temporary holding areas for objects surviving Minor GC
Long-term storage for objects promoted from Young Gen

items: Object Allocation Path: When an object is instantiated via the 'new' keyword, it is typically allocated in the Eden space. If Eden fills up, a Minor GC is triggered. Surviving objects are moved to the active Survivor space, and their age counter increments by one.

Survivor Space Swapping: At any given time, one Survivor space is active (destined to receive survivors) and the other is empty. During a Minor GC, surviving objects from Eden and the active Survivor space are copied to the empty Survivor space, and their roles swap for the next cycle.

Promotion Threshold (Tenuring): When an object's age exceeds the MaxTenuringThreshold, or if the cumulative size of objects in the Survivor space exceeds the SurvivorRatio threshold, the object is promoted into the Old Generation.

Card Tables and Remembered Sets: To collect the Young Generation without scanning the entire Old Generation for cross-generation object references, the JVM utilizes a Card Table. The Old Gen is divided into 512-byte cards; if an Old Gen object is modified to reference a Young Gen object, the corresponding card is marked 'dirty', allowing collectors to scan only modified regions.

parsed_answer.content: A classic production anti-pattern is 'premature promotion,' which occurs when the Young Generation or Survivor spaces are configured too small. If Survivor spaces fill up before objects reach their max tenuring age, the JVM is forced to promote young objects directly into the Old Generation. This prematurely clutters the Old Gen, triggering frequent, latency-spiking Full GCs. Always monitor promotion rates using metrics like JVM GC pause times and memory pools to appropriately tune -XX:NewRatio and -XX:SurvivorRatio.

title: Explain the Generational Garbage Collection model (Young Gen, Old/Tenured Gen).
